newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: U.N. says Guatemala human rights improve.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Guatemala human rights improve.

text.p: Guatemalans are no longer victims of state-sponsored violence but an inadequate justice system means they have no guarantee of due process, a U.N. mission said in a human rights report on Wednesday.
The report, covering the second half of 1996, is the sixth and final human rights report by the United Nations Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala (MINUGUA).

"The question is no longer protecting citizens from a state that systematically violates their rights. Now we are talking about a state that is not capable of protecting its own citizens," outgoing MINUGUA director David Stephen said.
MINUGUA was invited in 1994 to monitor human rights in Guatemala.

During more than three decades the Guatemalan army and military-controlled governments were blamed for a campaign of terror -- including torture, massacres and assassinations -- against all sources of opposition.
An estimated 100,000 people, mostly civilians, died in the war and an additional 40,000 disappeared.
Since the government and leftist rebels of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit signed a peace accord Dec. 29, MINUGUA no longer verifies human rights.
The mission will take on a new role overseeing implementation of a group of peace accords, including Indian rights and reductions in the army.
MINUGUA accepted 1,665 complaints of rights violations against 10,409 people in 1995. The number of complaints the mission accepted for investigation dropped to 891 against 4,594 people in 1996.
